source.title: Empirical Evaluation of Progressive Coding for Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: No evident file problem; the full paper text is present, with some equation and text-extraction artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: Evaluates sparse-autoencoder representations of Gemma-2-2b activations, extending indirect evidence about SAE features to an LLM setting. It does not reproduce the toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper tests progressive SAE reconstruction and SAE-feature interpretability on LLM activations, and measures importance and activation distributions in SAE dictionaries. It does not test toy networks, neuron polysemanticity, or whether superposition is the mechanism behind these results. Permutation rankings used to order features and other hyperparameter choices are not treated as outcomes.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper on progressive-coding SAEs for Gemma-2-2b. It uses SAEs as a tool and reports its own methods' performance (Matryoshka SAEs, column permutation) against baseline SAEs. The power-law results describe SAE dictionary statistics, not whether LLM activations hold superposed sparse features. Feature splitting is invoked to explain a performance drop ('likely attributable'), not measured. No result bears on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with refinements. The authors propose a dictionary power law for SAEs and say it holds across sizes. They find Matryoshka SAEs give lower reconstruction loss, better recaptured LM loss and higher RSA than pruned (permuted) vanilla SAEs, while pruned vanilla SAEs are more interpretable. They attribute the reduced benefit at low granularity-to-size ratios to feature splitting, which they flag as a limitation for distillation.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates sparse autoencoders on Gemma-2-2b activations, measures dictionary statistics and progressive reconstruction, and evaluates SAE-feature interpretability. It does not reproduce the toy-network setup or interventions of the original superposition work.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance depends on granularity relative to dictionary size; feature splitting makes truncation less effective at lower granularity-to-size ratios. Within Matryoshka SAEs, innermost features score higher than outermost features on simulation scoring.

fits_no_version.finding: In 16k/32k/65k TopK SAEs on Gemma-2-2b, decoder-covariance eigenvalues follow a power law (α -0.54 to -0.72, R2 ≈ 0.92). Activation magnitude and frequency follow approximate power laws with steeper tails.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionary feature importance follows a power law (dictionary power law hypothesis).

record.problems: Experiments use one LLM (Gemma-2-2b) and SAEs described as modest in size relative to recent work; the authors say validation at larger scales remains necessary. Some comparisons and interpretability outcomes are reported qualitatively or through figures, and the training distributions differ for the GemmaScope comparison. These results do not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical units of the model.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported row for the scaling-law fit, which measures reconstruction-loss scaling rather than the feature structure or recovery named by the tested versions. Figure-only per-condition values for reconstruction, RSA, and fuzzing were not transcribed where the text gives no separable values.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity-competition analysis.
Does not test whether Gemma-2-2b features are spread across neurons or are genuinely sparse features recovered by the SAE. It only evaluates SAE variants against each other.
Does not measure completeness, stability across runs or canonicity. Feature splitting is cited and posited, not measured.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' and its V4/V5 labels are not justified. Every evaluative row compares the authors' own progressive-coding methods, and the feature-splitting row rests on a cited phenomenon used as an explanation. Superposition is mentioned only as background motivation for SAEs.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-model experiment testing overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
No test of neuron polysemanticity or whether features compete for limited dimensions according to importance.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.

Does not establish that the SAE features are the LLM's underlying features, or that LLM features are distributed across neurons. Tests reconstruction and interpretability of SAE representations of one model's activations.

Reports feature splitting across SAE dictionary sizes, but does not test whether SAE features are complete or canonical in the model, nor their stability across training runs or other extraction methods.
Does not test whether the features underlying superposition are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: TopK SAEs (16k, 32k, and 65k)
rows.operation_detail: Measured eigenvalues of the decoder-matrix covariance and fitted a power law.

conditions.value: not stated in the reported result

rows.measure: Power-law fit to eigenvalues of decoder-matrix covariance
rows.value: Exponents (α) ranged from -0.54 to -0.72; R2 values ranged from 0.916 to 0.922.
rows.note: The paper interprets this as a hierarchy in the SAE feature space, with a small number of directions capturing most variance. The result is reported across the three SAE sizes, not separately for each.
rows.check: Measures the eigenvalue spectrum of the SAE decoder covariance, a property of the learned dictionary. It does not measure whether the LLM stores sparse features in superposition. This is a related construct; recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: TopK SAEs (16k, 32k, and 65k)
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean squared feature activations and fitted a power law.
rows.value: Approximate power-law exponents ranged from -1.03 to -1.27; R2 values ranged from 0.741 to 0.857. The tail decreased more steeply than a power law would predict.
rows.note: The approximate relationship applies in the middle range, with a stated deviation in the tail. The result is aggregated across the three sizes.
rows.check: A power-law fit to SAE activation magnitudes, a dictionary statistic rather than a test of V4. The 'partial' state reflects tail deviation from a power law, not partial support for any version.

rows.subject: TopK SAEs (16k, 32k, and 65k)
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature activation frequency and fitted a power law.
rows.value: Approximate power-law exponents ranged from -1.00 to -1.20; R2 values ranged from 0.868 to 0.887. The tail showed a sharp decline.
rows.note: The paper describes a frequency hierarchy but says the least-used features activate more rarely than a pure power law predicts. The result is aggregated across the three sizes.
rows.check: A power-law fit to SAE feature activation frequency, a dictionary statistic. It bears on no version.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAEs and baseline TopK SAEs
rows.operation_detail: Compared reconstruction fidelity across granularities at fixed relative sparsity.

conditions.value: {64, 128, 256, 512} active features as listed in Table 1

rows.baseline: Baseline TopK SAE and baseline column-permuted SAE
rows.value: The Matryoshka SAE outperformed both baselines at all granularities.
rows.note: The paper reports the comparative outcome in text but does not give the underlying per-granularity values there.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (Matryoshka SAE) with baselines on progressive reconstruction. This is method performance, not a result on the claim, and should not be a claim row.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAEs
rows.operation_detail: Compared full-capacity Matryoshka SAE performance with a baseline autoencoder of the same size.
rows.measure: Recaptured downstream cross-entropy loss and reconstruction loss
rows.baseline: Baseline autoencoder of the same size
rows.value: Matryoshka SAEs closely tracked the same-size baseline on both metrics.
rows.locator: Section 6; sparsity-versus-fidelity results text and Figures 9–10
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison, not separate numeric values for each size or metric.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method with a same-size baseline at full capacity. This is method performance, not a test of V4.

rows.subject: 65K Matryoshka SAE, 65K TopK permuted SAE, 32K SAE with reordering, and baseline TopK SAEs
rows.operation_detail: Compared performance using only the first n latents of larger SAEs with smaller SAEs.

conditions.value: 16K, 10K, or 32K first latents, as specified in the text
held-out evaluation; exact condition-specific sample count not restated

rows.baseline: SAE trained at the corresponding smaller size
rows.value: Using the first latents of a larger SAE gave performance comparable to training an SAE of that size from scratch. At 16K latents, the 65K Matryoshka and 65K TopK permuted SAEs outperformed a baseline 16K TopK SAE, but the 32K SAE with reordering outperformed them at 16K or 10K granularity.
rows.locator: Section 6; Figure 11 and accompanying Results text
rows.note: The paper says this advantage becomes less pronounced as the granularity-to-model-size ratio decreases, attributing the degradation to feature splitting.
rows.check: Compares truncated large SAEs with smaller SAEs, which is method performance. The feature-splitting explanation is an interpretation and is not measured.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated how well Llama-3-1-70B predicted SAE feature activations from generated feature explanations.

conditions.value: 10 test samples and 20 training samples for explanations

rows.measure: Pearson correlation between simulated and ground-truth feature activations
rows.baseline: Outer granularities of the Matryoshka SAE
rows.value: Mean correlation increased from 0.57 to 0.74 from outermost to innermost granularities.
rows.locator: Interpretability; Figure 12–13 and accompanying Results text
rows.note: The result concerns prediction of SAE activation values from explanations, not direct validation that SAE features are complete or canonical model units.
rows.check: Compares simulation-scoring interpretability across granularities inside the authors' Matryoshka SAE. This is own-method evaluation; the 0.57 to 0.74 values are not a test of V4.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compared automated simulation-scoring interpretability with other SAE types and a randomly initialized SAE.
rows.measure: Mean Pearson correlation of simulated and ground-truth activations
rows.baseline: Baseline TopK SAE; GemmaScope JumpReLU SAE; randomly initialized SAE
rows.value: Higher than the randomly initialized SAE, on par with GemmaScope, and below the baseline TopK SAE models.
rows.note: The paper provides these comparisons qualitatively, without numeric values in the text.
rows.check: Compares the own method's interpretability with TopK, GemmaScope and random SAEs. It is method comparison; the only above-random result is reported qualitatively.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAEs
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated feature explanations using token-level fuzzing.
rows.measure: Balanced accuracy for identifying tokens that activate features
rows.baseline: Average feature-quantile performance; exact numeric baseline not stated
rows.value: The Matryoshka SAEs slightly underperformed; first latents performed better than average, but scores dropped quickly.
rows.locator: Interpretability; Figure 14 and accompanying Results text
rows.note: The text reports the outcome qualitatively and does not provide balanced-accuracy values.
rows.check: Fuzzing evaluation of the own method, which bears on no version. The text gives no numeric values.

rows.subject: Smaller and larger SAE dictionaries
rows.operation_detail: Reported feature splitting as dictionary size grows.
rows.measure: Whether a basis vector remains a single feature as dictionary size grows
rows.value: A basis vector in a smaller SAE can be decomposed into multiple separate basis vectors in a larger SAE; the paper says selecting only the most important split features may fail to preserve the smaller SAE feature's complete functionality.
rows.locator: Section 6 Results; Appendix A, Feature Splitting; Section C, Limitations and Future Work
rows.note: This is evidence of size-dependent feature splitting, not a direct test of completeness or canonicity across runs or extraction methods.
rows.check: Feature splitting is defined and cited (Bricken et al.) and invoked as a 'likely' explanation for a performance drop. The paper never directly measures splitting across dictionary sizes, so this row is an interpretation or cited result, not a finding.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2b activations represented with the tested TopK and Matryoshka SAEs
reader_labels.reason: SAE dictionaries show hierarchical activation statistics, and progressive SAEs reconstruct the activations with reported fidelity and language-model performance; see r1–r7.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Automated interpretability evaluations of Matryoshka SAE features
reader_labels.reason: Simulation scoring is below the baseline TopK SAE, while fuzzing slightly underperforms and performance drops for later latents; see r8–r9.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Comparison of SAE dictionaries at different sizes
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that a feature in a smaller SAE can split into several features in a larger SAE, so feature identity and functionality need not be preserved across dictionary sizes; see r10.
